newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Premier puts nuclear appeal to Taiwan's people.
newsitem.headline: Premier puts nuclear appeal to Taiwan's people.

text.p: Taiwan's premier, barred by the opposition from defending a controversial nuclear power project in parliament, appealed directly for public support on Thursday on the eve of a do-or-die vote.
"We cannot have such important national projects being stopped every two or three days," Premier Lien Chan said of the partially built but politically stalemated nuclear plant.
"This project was approved after many years of careful consideration. We must have an appropriate scale of nuclear power," Lien said in his live television and radio appeal.
"The government has a responsibility to carry it out."

Parliament humiliated the cabinet in May by cancelling funds for the island's US$4.1 billion fourth nuclear power station, but state utility Taiwan Power has pushed ahead anyway and the cabinet lodged a formal appeal with the body in June.
Opponents can make the cancellation stand only by mustering a two-thirds majority in Friday's final parliamentary vote.
Hanging in the balance, among other things, is U.S. giant General Electric's US$1.8 billion contract to supply the light-water plant's twin reactors and generators.

Lawmakers from the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party tried to kill the project on Tuesday by forming human walls and physically preventing Lien from entering parliament to explain his cabinet's appeal and defend the project.
Under parliamentary rules, debate of such a defence must precede a vote, but ruling Nationalist Party lawmakers met the requirement by having Lien's report read into the record.
The body, where the Nationalists have a scant 51 percent majority, voted on Thursday to skip further debate.

Leaving nothing to chance, Lien turned up the pressure on the opposition by making his defence to the public, summoning reporters on short notice to a podium outside the cabinet's Taipei headquarters.
"This is a choice we cannot afford not to make," Lien said, arguing that failing to finish the plant would tarnish Taiwan's reputation and weaken his government.
"This will cause great uncertainty in the administration of government," said Lien. "It will damage our international image and the government's image."
Lien had slammed the Democratic Progressive Party's strong-arm tactics on Tuesday as a "dark day for democracy".

Lien said Taiwan must diversify and widen its energy sources to ensure stable power supplies for its economic development. He dismissed environmental criticisms, saying a state-of-the-art nuclear plant was far cleaner than those burning carbon fuels.
Suggesting a possible compromise, Lien hinted Taipei would not seek to build further nuclear plants.
"Judging from Taiwan's natural environment and society's responses, the chances are very small for us to build a fifth nuclear power plant," Lien said.
Lien, a lightning rod for opposition attacks, said calls in his own party for a further two-month delay even if parliament backs the plant were unwarranted and would be costly.
General Electric turned up the heat on Wednesday by saying it would seek unspecified compensation if construction were delayed beyond a deadline that passed at midnight the same day.
Taiwan Power has continued work despite the deadlock, saying it regarded the project alive unless the state appeal is rejected.
The utility already has sunk US$220 million into preliminary work on the 2,700-megawatt nuclear station north of Taipei.
